enquiry: Our dairy process includes a relatively clear whey stream before a concentration stage. We want to investigate whether spectroscopy can track protein concentration as the stream changes, with laboratory results used as the reference. The stream can become more turbid under some operating conditions. We need a first measurement concept that handles this change rather than assuming the liquid always remains clear.

clarification_questions.question: What goes wrong today with the protein concentration in the whey stream, and what decision would real-time protein data drive at the concentration stage?
clarification_questions.why: Clarifies the stakeholder pain and the process decision that the measurement must support.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Decision and pain unknown; the first step is to confirm the process decision before choosing a method.

clarification_questions.question: What is the expected protein concentration range in the whey stream, stated as ppm or %?
clarification_questions.why: Determines whether the method must detect trace or major component levels, which affects method choice and lab screening design.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Level unknown; lab screening establishes whether it is ppm or % level.

clarification_questions.question: How turbid does the whey stream become under the operating conditions that cause change, and which conditions cause it?
clarification_questions.why: Turbidity range determines the probe geometry (transmission, transflection, diffuse reflection or ATR) and whether one method remains robust across the change.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Turbidity range unknown; lab screening on representative clear and turbid samples establishes the probe geometry needed.

clarification_questions.question: What are the temperature, flow, fouling and cleaning conditions of the whey stream, and how do the composition and particle or fat content vary?
clarification_questions.why: Temperature, fouling and composition variation change the spectra and can invalidate a calibration.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Process conditions unknown; the calibration must be tested across the expected variation in the lab screening.

clarification_questions.question: Where would the measurement be installed, can the probe contact the stream, and how far is the analyzer from the measuring point? Are any optical fibers already installed?
clarification_questions.why: Installation point and distance determine whether a fiber link is needed and which fiber types can carry the required wavelengths.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Installation point and distance unknown; a fiber link is assumed to be needed until confirmed.

clarification_questions.question: What is the current laboratory reference method for protein, how often are samples taken, and what is its accuracy?
clarification_questions.why: The reference method and its accuracy set the achievable calibration quality and the sampling plan for time-aligned spectra and reference values.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Reference method and accuracy unknown; the expert confirms them before any calibration is built.

clarification_questions.question: What accuracy, response time and budget are required for the first measurement concept?
clarification_questions.why: Requirements decide whether a single method or a combined concept is justified and set the scope of the feasibility plan.
clarification_questions.assumption_if_unanswered: Requirements unknown; a single-method lab screening is proposed first, with the simplest adequate option preferred.

flags_before_revision.detail: not_supported: The claim says silica fibers suit Raman, but S02 p.6 lists silica fiber ranges only for UV-VIS (190-1200 nm) and VIS-NIR (350-2400 nm) and never mentions Raman. The Raman suitability is not stated on the cited page. Fix: Limit the claim to the fiber ranges shown on S02 p.6 (silica for UV-VIS and VIS-NIR; IR fibers for the longer-wavelength range) and drop the Raman statement, or cite a source page that explicitly covers Raman fiber use.

not_supported: S01 p.10 says NIR bands overlap and that chemometrics are used for quantitative analysis. It does not mention whey, composition or matrix changes, or calibration invalidation. Fix: Rephrase as a general chemometric risk: NIR quantification relies on PLS calibration models (S01 p.17), so the models need checking when the sample matrix changes. Cite S01 p.10 and S01 p.17 for that, and drop the whey-specific claim unless a source page supports it.

not_supported: S01 p.17 and p.18 say scattering interferes with spectra (corrected with MSC or SNV) and that turbid milk is harder for transmission. Neither page says temperature changes or turbidity can mimic protein changes. Fix: Restrict the risk to what the pages show: scattering from turbidity or particle size can interfere with the spectra and needs correction (MSC/SNV, S01 p.17), and strongly turbid milk prevents light penetration in transmission (S01 p.18). Remove the temperature and protein-mimicry statements or source them to an AFS page that covers them.
